as_told.title: Marconi's transatlantic signal bounced off the ionosphere

plain: This story is about Guglielmo Marconi, the radio pioneer, who in the early 1900s sent a radio signal across the Atlantic from Cornwall in England to Newfoundland in Canada. Filippo Biondi, a scientist who has used radar to scan beneath the pyramids, says on Jesse Michels' podcast that it worked by luck. According to him, Marconi's radio waves bounced off the ionosphere, an electrically charged layer high in the sky, and zigzagged down to the receiver, just as the theory of electromagnetism describes. Michels later retells it, saying Marconi was ignorant in a useful way, because he simply tried it across the ocean without knowing it shouldn't work. They tell it to show that a bold experiment can succeed even when the experts say it can't.
